name: Colonial
lede: Colonial is a dark, grayish navy that Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary filed under fashion and textiles; the books say nothing about the color itself, though a good deal about the blue dye trade its name recalls.

sections.title: A name from a 1930 dictionary
sections.body:
Colonial is a name from Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color*, which lists it on plate 39, position C 12, with a first recorded use of 1921 [1]. Our library classes it under fashion and textiles, and no other source in it carries the name [1]. The swatch is measured from a scan of the 1930 plate, so it is approximate [1].

The nearest named colors are [[navy]], 6.0 units away, and [[dusky-blue]] [1]. Who coined the name, and what it was meant to evoke, is undocumented in our sources [1].

sections.title: What the books do say
sections.body:
We found no passage in the 29 books that describes a color called Colonial [2]. In the roughly forty passages we read, the word is an adjective for a period or an empire, as in colonial roads, colonial plantations and colonial rule [2].

The blue connection is real but indirect. Ball notes that in the 1880s a major dyestuff of the world, indigo, still came from India under British colonial rule, and it was the most profitable of the empire's activities in Asia [3]. In 1870 India had 2,800 indigo factories, and the dye went into mass-produced goods such as military uniforms [3]. Balfour-Paul describes the trade as tied to colonial farming based on slavery, and notes that when Britain cut off tropical indigo, Napoleon offered rewards for a local substitute for his army's uniforms [4]. Nothing in our sources links Maerz and Paul's name to that trade, so read the link as context, not as origin [1][3][4]. The deep blues it points toward are [[indigo]] and [[prussian-blue]].

One dictionary entry does tie a blue to the period. Paterson's *Jersey blue* names the blue worn by soldiers from New Jersey in the colonial period [5]. At Colonial Williamsburg in Virginia, which Finlay calls a center for eighteenth-century paint technology, historical houses are painted to match their period [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 92 works, 0.39 per cent of the archive [7]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color and not a pigment test [7].

It has two homes. The first dated match is Taddeo Gaddi's [[painting:commons-Q3842751|Madonna and Child Enthroned with Angels and Saints]] (1355), and the 1300s and 1400s run at about twice the archive rate [7]. Then the 1900s run at 5.25 times it, with 34 of 1,674 paintings, and the 1920s are the peak decade with 5 of 237 [7]. The painters who use it most include Vilhelm Lundstrøm (4 of 17 paintings), [[painter:henri-matisse|Matisse]] (5 of 50) and [[painter:auguste-renoir|Renoir]] (3 of 50) [7].

The largest patches are in Bronzino's [[painting:commons-Q48814933|Portrait of a girl]] (1545, 40 per cent of the canvas) and Jawlensky's [[painting:nga-54131|Murnau]] (1910, 38 per cent) [7]. Inside a painting it is a shadow in 75 per cent of cases and a mid-tone in the other 25 per cent [7]. It keeps company with navy, charcoal and gunmetal [7].

This dark blue lives in two eras of our paintings, the 1300s and 1400s and then the 1900s, where it runs at 5 times the archive rate.
